chapterTitle: III. The Motor System, Spinal Cord & Lesions

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The cerebral hemispheres contain deep grey matter nuclei such as the basal ganglia and thalamus. In the spinal cord, grey matter is central and H-shaped. The brainstem has grey matter surrounded by white matter, and the cerebellar cortex is grey matter externally.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral hemispheres contain deep grey matter nuclei; spinal cord grey matter is central, white matter peripheral
options: In spinal cord, white matter is H-shaped.
In brain stem, white matter surrounds grey matter.
Cerebral hemispheres contain deep nuclei formed of grey matter.
In cerebellum, white matter forms the outer cortex.
In spinal cord, grey matter surrounds white matter.

questions.text: For each tract in the left column, choose the appropriate description in the right column:
questions.explanation: This matching question tests knowledge of descending motor pathways: vestibulospinal tract extends through the whole spinal cord to facilitate anti-gravity extensors; pontine reticulospinal only reaches mid-thoracic level.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibulospinal extends full length of cord

pairs.target: Facilitatory to muscle tone of flexor muscle group.
Extensor to antigravity muscles & descend within the whole length of the spinal cord.
Extensor to antigravity muscles & does not extend beyond mid-thoracic region.
Turning of head & neck in response to auditory & visual stimuli.

questions.text: Enumerate nuclei of anterior horn of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The anterior horn contains motor nuclei organized somatotopically: Medial motor nuclei (medial column) supply muscles of neck and trunk; Lateral motor nuclei (lateral column) supply limb muscles, divided into anterior lateral (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius), posterior lateral (forearm flexors), and postural (limb extensors). The phrenic nucleus at C3,4,5 supplies the diaphragm. These are lower motor neuron cell bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn motor nuclei: medial, lateral (with subdivisions), and phrenic nucleus
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclei of anterior horn: (1) Medial motor nuclei - in medial column, supply muscles of neck and trunk; (2) Lateral motor nuclei - in lateral column, supply limb muscles; (a) Anterior lateral (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius); (b) Posterior lateral (flexors of forearm); (c) Postural (extensors of limb); (3) Phrenic nucleus (C3,4,5) - supplies diaphragm.

questions.text: Posterior external arcuate fibers are axons of:
questions.explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers originate from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus), which receives proprioceptive input from the upper limb. These fibers enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus gives posterior arcuate fibers

questions.text: Describe inferior olivary complex.
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary complex consists of: (1) MAIN OLIVARY NUCLEUS - folded gray matter receiving input from red nucleus, spinal cord, and cerebral cortex; (2) MEDIAL ACCESSORY OLIVARY NUCLEUS; (3) DORSAL ACCESSORY OLIVARY NUCLEUS. OUTPUT: Olivocerebellar fibers cross and enter cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. FUNCTION: Involved in motor learning, coordination, and timing. Lesions cause intention tremor.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary complex: main, medial accessory, dorsal accessory nuclei; olivocerebellar fibers via inferior cerebellar peduncle
questions.modelAnswer: NUCLEI OF GSE COLUMN: (1) OCULOMOTOR NUCLEUS (III) - superior, inferior, medial rectus, inferior oblique; (2) TROCHLEAR NUCLEUS (IV) - superior oblique; (3) ABDUCENT NUCLEUS (VI) - lateral rectus; (4) HYPOGLOSSAL NUCLEUS (XII) - intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles (except palatoglossus by X).

questions.text: A protruded tongue which deviates to the right and shows wasting and fasciculations indicates a lesion in:
questions.explanation: Hypoglossal nerve palsy produces lower motor neuron signs in the tongue: the tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion when protruded, and there is wasting and fasciculations (spontaneous twitching of muscle fibers) on the affected side. This is because the genioglossus muscle on the affected side is weak and cannot push the tongue forward symmetrically. In contrast, upper motor neuron lesions produce tongue deviation away from the lesion side, without wasting or fasciculations.
questions.keyConcept: LMN hypoglossal lesion causes tongue deviation to the SAME side with wasting and fasciculations.

questions.text: For the Anterior limb of the internal capsule, choose its appropriate statement from the right column.
questions.explanation: The anterior limb of the internal capsule lies between the head of the caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus (putamen + globus pallidus) laterally. It contains frontopontine fibers (corticofugal from frontal lobe to pontine nuclei) and thalamocortical fibers to the frontal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior limb of internal capsule = between caudate head and lentiform nucleus; contains frontopontine fibers.

pairs.target: Lies between head of caudate nucleus & lentiform nucleus.

questions.text: For the Genu of the internal capsule, choose its appropriate statement from the right column.
questions.explanation: The genu (knee) of the internal capsule is the bend between the anterior and posterior limbs, located at the level of the interventricular foramen. It contains corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibers that control voluntary movement of the contralateral face, tongue, and throat, as well as some corticospinal fibers for the neck.
questions.keyConcept: Genu of internal capsule contains corticonuclear fibers for contralateral face/tongue/pharynx movement.

questions.text: For the Posterior limb of the internal capsule, choose its appropriate statement from the right column.
questions.explanation: The posterior limb of the internal capsule lies between the thalamus/medial globus pallidus medially and the posterior limb of the lentiform nucleus laterally. It contains the corticospinal tract (for body and limbs), thalamocortical sensory radiations, and corticopontine fibers. Most fibers pass through the genu and posterior limb.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior limb of internal capsule contains corticospinal tract (body/limb) and thalamocortical sensory radiations.

questions.text: The spinal tract involved with the control of trunk muscles is:
questions.explanation: The anterior corticospinal tract descends from the motor cortex in the lateral column but then crosses in the spinal cord (anterior white commissure) and supplies the TRUNK muscles (axial and proximal limb muscles). It is involved in fine control of trunk posture and proximal limb movements. The lateral corticospinal tract controls limb muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior corticospinal tract controls axial/trunk muscles; decussates in spinal cord. Lateral corticospinal tract controls limb muscles.

questions.text: A 32-year-old male patient presents with a loss of lower extremity motor control on the left side. He exhibits a Babinski sign and has increased deep tendon reflexes in the left lower extremity. He has no loss of sensation. The structure lesioned in the spinal cord is the:
questions.explanation: Left lower limb motor weakness with Babinski sign and increased deep tendon reflexes (UMN signs) indicates a lesion of the LEFT lateral corticospinal tract. The corticospinal tract decussates in the medulla (pyramidal decussation), so a lesion below this level affects the IPSILATERAL side below the lesion. Left corticospinal tract lesion causes left-sided weakness.
questions.keyConcept: Left corticospinal tract lesion = LEFT lower limb weakness with UMN signs (Babinski, hyperreflexia); tract decussates in medulla.

questions.text: 24-year-old man was brought to the ER following a driving accident. Neurological testing revealed paraplegia and loss of all sensory modalities in bilateral lower limbs. Sensation for the upper limbs and the trunk was intact. Which of the following might be the nature and location of the lesion in this patient?
questions.explanation: The presentation of bilateral lower limb paralysis with intact upper limbs and trunk suggests central cord syndrome. Option C is correct because complete transection at T8 would paralyze everything below T8 (including trunk). Option E (central cord syndrome) is typically at C5-C6 levels and affects upper limbs more than lower due to the somatotopic arrangement of the corticospinal tract. The patient has paraplegia with intact upper limbs, which is most consistent with a T8 cord lesion where the corticospinal fibers for lower limbs are most affected.
questions.keyConcept: Central cord syndrome preferentially affects upper extremities due to the somatotopic organization of corticospinal fibers in the spinal cord.
options: Complete section of spinal cord at C8 level
Hemi section of spinal cord at C8 level
Complete section of spinal cord at T8 level
Hemi section of spinal cord at T8 level

questions.text: What does lesion of Area 4 cause?
questions.explanation: Lesion of Area 4 (primary motor cortex) causes contralateral hemiplegia, most affecting fine skilled movements of the distal limbs. The face and hand representations are most affected due to their large cortical areas.
questions.keyConcept: Area 4 lesion: contralateral hemiplegia, especially fine movements (face, hand). UMN signs below lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral hemiplegia especially affecting fine skilled movements. The paralysis is most pronounced in the distal parts of the contralateral limbs (especially hand and foot), with spasticity and hyperreflexia (upper motor neuron signs).

questions.text: Which tract forms the external arcuate fibers?
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract forms the external arcuate fibers. These fibers arise from the accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus and enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, carrying unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract: from accessory cuneate nucleus → external arcuate fibers → cerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: The cuneocerebellar tract. Its fibers arise from the accessory cuneate nucleus and form the external arcuate fibers that enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, carrying unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.

questions.text: What is the effect of spinal cord complete transverse section?
questions.explanation: Complete transverse section of the spinal cord produces bilateral paralysis below the level of injury. Location determines outcome: above C5 = fatal (respiratory failure); C5-T1 = quadriplegia; below T1 = paraplegia.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord transection: above C5 = death; C5-T1 = quadriplegia; below T1 = paraplegia.
questions.modelAnswer: Above C5: death due to respiratory paralysis. Between C5 and T1: quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs). Below T1: paraplegia (paralysis of lower limbs only).

questions.text: Mention 4 afferent fibers of the ICP.
questions.explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle (ICP) carries afferent fibers: posterior spinocerebellar tract, dorsal external arcuate fibers (from accessory cuneate nucleus), ventral external arcuate fibers (from arcuate nucleus), and olivocerebellar fibers (from inferior olivary nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: ICP afferents: posterior spinocerebellar, dorsal/ventral external arcuate, olivocerebellar fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior spinocerebellar tracts (proprioception from trunk), dorsal external arcuate fibers (from accessory cuneate nucleus - upper limb proprioception), ventral external arcuate fibers (from arcuate nucleus), and olivocerebellar fibers (from inferior olivary nucleus - climbing fibers).

questions.text: Mention the efferent fibers of the ICP.
questions.explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries efferent fibers: cerebellovestibular fibers (to vestibular nuclei), cerebelloreticular fibers (to reticular formation), and cerebelloolivary fibers (to inferior olivary nucleus). These complete feedback loops.
questions.keyConcept: ICP efferents: cerebellovestibular, cerebelloreticular, cerebelloolivary fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: Cerebellovestibular fibers (to vestibular nuclei), cerebello reticular fibers (to reticular formation), and cerebello olivary fibers (to inferior olivary nucleus). These form feedback pathways from cerebellum to brainstem.

questions.text: Mention the afferent fiber of the MCP.
questions.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) carries only afferent fibers - the corticopontocerebellar fibers. These arise from the cerebral cortex, pass through the basilar pons, and enter the cerebellum as the MCP. There are no efferent fibers in the MCP.
questions.keyConcept: MCP: afferent only. Corticopontocerebellar fibers from cerebral cortex through pons to cerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer: Cortico ponto cerebellar fibers. These arise from the cerebral cortex, synapse in the pontine nuclei, cross to the contralateral side, and enter the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle.

questions.text: Mention the afferent fibers of the SCP.
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP) carries afferent fibers: the anterior spinocerebellar tract (proprioception from lower limb) and the tectocerebellar tract (from superior colliculus for visual reflexes).
questions.keyConcept: SCP afferents: anterior spinocerebellar tract, tectocerebellar tract.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinocerebellar tract (carrying proprioceptive information from the lower limbs and trunk) and tecto-cerebellar tract (carrying visual and auditory information from the superior colliculus).

questions.text: Loss of fine voluntary movements is most likely caused by a lesion in which area?
questions.explanation: Loss of fine voluntary movements (dexterity) indicates damage to the corticospinal tract or its origin in the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex), which mediates fractionated finger movements.
questions.keyConcept: Fine finger movements require intact corticospinal function at the precentral gyrus.

questions.text: Which muscle is supplied only by contralateral corticobulbar fibers?
questions.explanation: The lower face (chin, lips below the mouth) receives only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Upper face muscles (frontalis, orbicularis oculi) receive bilateral innervation.
questions.keyConcept: Lower facial muscles are innervated only by the contralateral motor cortex, unlike upper face muscles.
options: Muscles of the upper part of the face

questions.text: Which facial muscle receives only contralateral cortical innervation?
questions.explanation: The mentalis muscle (chin) receives only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Other lower facial muscles receive partial bilateral innervation, which is why upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral only innervation of lower face muscles distinguishes UMN from LMN facial palsy.
options: Orbicularis oculi of the upper face
Orbicularis oris of the lower face

questions.text: Hemisection of the spinal cord most likely produces which finding?
questions.explanation: Spinal cord hemisection produces the classic Brown-Sequard pattern: ipsilateral upper motor neuron paralysis, loss of proprioception and vibration sense, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning a few segments below.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection causes classic Brown-Sequard syndrome with dissociated sensory loss and UMN signs.
options: Loss of all types of sensation of the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Loss of proprioception of the opposite side below the level of the lesion
Loss of dorsal column sensations of the same side below the level of the lesion
Lower motor neuron lesion of the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Upper motor neuron lesion of the opposite side at the level of the lesion

questions.text: Grey matter is .......... While white matter is ...........
questions.explanation: Grey matter (cell bodies) is centrally located in the spinal cord while white matter (myelinated fibers) is peripherally located, the reverse of the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Grey vs white matter distribution

questions.text: ........... means sensation of movement, vibration, position
questions.explanation: Proprioception encompasses the sensation of movement (kinesthesia), vibration, and joint/limb position, mediated by muscle spindles, tendon organs, and joint receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception definition

questions.text: All receptors of proprioception except:
questions.explanation: Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, tendon spindles (Golgi tendon organs), and joint receptors; Merkel discs are tactile receptors, not proprioceptive.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception receptors

questions.text: All the following paired tract except:
questions.explanation: The sulcomarginal tract is a descending motor tract in the anterior column, not a paired bilateral tract like vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, and tectospinal.
questions.keyConcept: Unpaired tracts

questions.text: All the following direct tract except:
questions.explanation: Lateral reticulospinal and rubrospinal tracts are indirect (multineuronal) tracts, while olivespinal, vestibulospinal, ventral reticulospinal, and sulcomarginal are direct.
questions.keyConcept: Direct vs indirect tracts
options: ventral reticulo-spinal tract and sulco-marginal tract

questions.text: All those tract end in all level of spinal cord except:
questions.explanation: Rubrospinal and ventral vestibulospinal tracts do NOT extend to all spinal levels; lateral vestibulospinal, sulcomarginal, and reticulospinal do.
questions.keyConcept: Tract termination levels

questions.text: Molecular layer Contains all the following except:
questions.explanation: The molecular layer contains outer stellate cells, inner basket cells, Purkinje cell dendrites, Golgi cell dendrites, and parallel fibers (Granular cell axons); mossy fibers are in the granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar molecular layer contents
options: Mossy fiber, dendrite of granular cell

questions.text: Large pyriform multipolar Cell:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are large pyriform (pear-shaped) multipolar neurons with a characteristic flask-shaped cell body and extensive dendritic tree.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cell morphology

questions.text: -- Contains T-shaped axon in Molecular layer:
questions.explanation: Granular cells have T-shaped axons (parallel fibers) that run tangentially in the molecular layer, forming excitatory synapses with Purkinje cell dendrites.
questions.keyConcept: Granular cell axon

questions.text: Cerebral medulla contain all the following except:
questions.explanation: The cerebral medulla contains afferent/efferent fibers, dentate nuclei, and Purkinje fiber axons; Purkinje cells themselves are in the cerebellar cortex, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral medulla contents

questions.text: Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Grey matter is central in spinal cord with neuron cell bodies; white matter is peripheral with myelinated fibers; the CNS lacks connective tissue framework.
questions.keyConcept: Grey white matter distribution

questions.text: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains neuron cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers; the distribution depends on myelin location.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin and matter distribution

questions.text: One of the followings is not present in grey matter:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated fibers; myelinated nerve fibers are found in white matter.
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter composition

questions.text: One of the following is a character of lumbar level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Lumbar level has the smallest white matter/grey matter ratio because it has relatively less white matter (fewer descending motor fibers passing through).
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar spinal cord
options: Smallest white matter / grey matter ratio.

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of cervical level of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Cervical spinal cord has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains the most descending and ascending fibers passing to/from the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical spinal cord
options: Has largest white matter/grey matter ratio.

questions.text: Receptor/s for proprioception is/are:
questions.explanation: Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors (Pacinian corpuscles at joints), providing limb position sense.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception receptors

questions.text: Anterior external arcuate fibres connect:
questions.explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate fibers
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the spinal cord.

questions.text: Posterior external arcuate fibres connect:
questions.explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers connect the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior external arcuate fibers
options: Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the cerebellum.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the opposite side with the spinal cord.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei of the same side with the spinal cord.

questions.text: One of the following is true about climbing fibres:
questions.explanation: Each climbing fiber forms powerful excitatory synapses with multiple Purkinje cell dendrites; one Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fiber Purkinje relationship
options: Each fibre synapse with one Purkinje cell.

questions.text: Which receptor has a motor efferent supply?
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles contain intrafusal fibers with gamma motor neuron innervation that adjusts sensitivity, unlike other receptors listed which are purely sensory.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle motor supply

questions.text: The Golgi tendon organ differs from the muscle spindle in that it:
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs lack gamma motor innervation (unlike muscle spindles), are in series with muscle, and detect tension; both have capsules.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon organ

questions.text: Gamma motor neurons are found in which lamina of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons are located in Rexed lamina IX of the anterior horn, innervating intrafusal muscle fibers within muscle spindles.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neuron location

questions.text: Tract forming external arcuate fibers:
questions.explanation: The external arcuate fibers arise from the cuneate nucleus and carry proprioceptive information to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: External arcuate fiber origin
questions.modelAnswer: The external arcuate fibers (cerebellar climbing fibers) arise from the olivary nuclei, particularly the inferior olivary nucleus. They pass through the hilum of the inferior olivary nucleus and cross the midline to reach the contralateral cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.text: Tracts ending on alpha and gamma neurons of extensors:
questions.explanation: Extensor muscles are controlled by lateral vestibulospinal (facilitates extensors) and medial reticulospinal tracts via gamma neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Extensor motor control
questions.modelAnswer: Vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts.

questions.text: Complete transverse section:
questions.explanation: A complete spinal cord transection produces different clinical pictures depending on level: above C5 causes respiratory death; between C5-T1 causes quadriplegia; below T1 causes paraplegia.
questions.keyConcept: Complete cord section effects vary by level: quadriplegia (C5-T1), paraplegia (below T1).
questions.modelAnswer: Above C5: death; Between C5-T1: quadriplegia; Below T1: paraplegia.

questions.text: 4 afferent fibers of ICP:
questions.explanation: The four afferent fibers of the inferior cerebellar peduncle are: posterior spinocerebellar, dorsal external arcuate, ventral external arcuate, and olivocerebellar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: ICP afferents: posterior spinocerebellar, both arcuate, olivocerebellar.
questions.modelAnswer: Posterior spinocerebellar, dorsal external arcuate, ventral external arcuate, olivocerebellar.

questions.text: Afferent fiber of MCP:
questions.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle carries corticopontocerebellar fibers, the largest afferent pathway to the cerebellum, originating from the pontine nuclei receiving cerebral cortex input.
questions.keyConcept: MCP afferent is corticopontocerebellar pathway from pons.
questions.modelAnswer: Corticopontocerebellar fibers.

questions.text: Afferent fibers of SCP:
questions.explanation: Afferent fibers of the superior cerebellar peduncle include anterior spinocerebellar fibers (carrying proprioceptive data from lower body) and tectocerebellar fibers (from superior colliculus).
questions.keyConcept: SCP afferents: anterior spinocerebellar and tectocerebellar fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior spinocerebellar, tectocerebellar.

questions.text: Efferent fibers of SCP:
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle carries four efferent pathways: fastigioreticular, cerebellorubral, dentatothalamic, and dentatorubrothalamic fibers projecting to thalamus and brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: SCP efferents: fastigioreticular, cerebellorubral, dentatothalamic, dentatorubrothalamic.
questions.modelAnswer: Fastigioreticular, cerebellorubral, dentatothalamic, dentatorubrothalamic.

questions.text: 3 external features of ventral medulla:
questions.explanation: The ventral medulla's three external features are the pyramid (motor decussation), olive (olivary nucleus), and inferior cerebellar peduncle containing ascending sensory fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral medulla features: pyramid, olive, inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer: The three external features of the ventral (anterior) medulla are: (1) Pyramids — longitudinal ridges containing corticospinal fibers; (2) Olivary prominences — formed by the underlying inferior olivary nuclei; (3) Ventral lateral sulcus — between the pyramid and olive, from which the hypoglossal nerve emerges.

questions.text: 3 elevations of closed medulla:
questions.explanation: The closed medulla (above the obex) displays three posterior elevations: the gracile tubercle (medial), cuneate tubercle (lateral), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the most lateral position.
questions.keyConcept: Closed medulla elevations: gracile, cuneate, inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer: The three elevations of the closed medulla are: (1) Medial eminence (fasciculus gracilis) — medial, overlying the gracile nucleus; (2) Sulcomarginal area — lateral to the medial eminence; (3) Inferior olivary swelling — the prominent olive formed by the inferior olivary nucleus laterally.

questions.text: Lateral boundaries:
questions.explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle consist of the superior cerebellar peduncle superiorly, the inferior cerebellar peduncle and gracile/cuneate tracts inferiorly, and the lateral recess extending toward the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral boundaries: SCP above, ICP and dorsal columns below, lateral recess.
questions.modelAnswer: Superiorly: SCP; Inferiorly: ICP + gracile and cuneate tracts; Lateral recess.

questions.text: Which of the following is a common microscopic feature between muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ?
questions.explanation: Both muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs are encapsulated receptors with connective tissue capsules surrounding their sensory endings, distinguishing them from free nerve endings.
questions.keyConcept: Both muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ are encapsulated receptors.
options: They are both present in series with extrafusal fibres.
They both respond only to active contraction.

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of the cervical level of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The cervical spinal cord has the largest white matter-to-grey matter ratio among spinal cord levels because it contains the most descending and ascending fiber tracts connecting the brain to all body regions.
questions.keyConcept: Cervical cord has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio.
options: Has the largest white matter/grey matter ratio
Contains the central canal in a ventral position

questions.text: The first order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is located in:
questions.explanation: Proprioception from the lower body is carried by first-order neurons whose cell bodies are located in the spinal (dorsal root) ganglia, where peripheral receptors from muscle spindles and tendon organs synapse.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception first-order neuron: spinal (dorsal root) ganglia.

questions.text: Which of the following is a rapid, monosynaptic reflex that helps maintain muscle length?
questions.explanation: The stretch (myotatic) reflex is a monosynaptic reflex mediated by muscle spindles that detects changes in muscle length and rapidly adjusts muscle tone to maintain posture.
questions.keyConcept: Stretch reflex: monosynaptic reflex maintaining muscle length.

questions.text: A patient has weakness of the right lower face, but can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Preserved forehead wrinkling indicates intact upper motor neuron (UMN) innervation to the facial nucleus's upper face region; weakness of only the lower face indicates a UMN lesion affecting the contralateral corticobulbar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Lower face weakness with spared forehead: contralateral corticobulbar (UMN) lesion.

questions.text: The muscle spindle is stretched by contraction of which fibres?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within the spindle, and when activated, they contract these fibers, stretching the sensory region and increasing spindle sensitivity to muscle stretch.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons stretch intrafusal fibers, increasing muscle spindle sensitivity.

questions.text: Rootlets of glossopharyngeal nerve lie:
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve rootlets emerge from the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla, which lies between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: CN IX between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle
options: Between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
Between lower border of pons and medulla.

questions.text: Connects the vestibular nuclei with cranial nuclei of III, IV, & VI:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome includes: contralateral hemiparesis (pyramidal tract), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue paralysis (hypoglossal nerve).
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome - contralateral weakness and proprioception loss

questions.text: Lesion of facial nerve at stylomastoid foramen leads to:
questions.explanation: A lesion at stylomastoid foramen causes lower motor neuron facial paralysis affecting all muscles on that side, including the forehead (loss of frontalis and orbicularis oculi).
questions.keyConcept: Stylomastoid lesion: LMN facial paralysis (entire ipsilateral face).
options: Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral anterior 2/3 of tongue.
Motor loss on the contralateral half of the face.
Motor loss on the ipsilateral half of face.
Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral half of soft palate.

questions.text: Describe dorsal surface of midbrain.
questions.explanation: The dorsal surface of the midbrain (tectum) shows the quadrigeminal plate (corpora quadrigemina): (1) SUPERIOR COLLICULI - visual reflexes (paired); (2) INFERIOR COLLICULI - auditory pathway. Below the inferior colliculi are the superior cerebellar peduncles. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally, emerging between the two inferior colliculi.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal midbrain: quadrigeminal plate (superior and inferior colliculi); CN IV exits dorsally
questions.modelAnswer: STRUCTURES IN BASIS PONTIS: (1) Longitudinal fibers - corticopontine, corticospinal, corticobulbar; (2) Transverse fibers - pontocerebellar fibers linking pons with cerebellum; (3) Pontine nuclei - gray matter between fiber bundles; (4) Basilar artery runs in basilar sulcus; (5) CN V attaches at lateral surface.

questions.text: Sections In lower level of pons show.
questions.explanation: Sections at the lower level of pons show the MIDDLE cerebellar peduncle (the largest cerebellar peduncle, connecting pons to cerebellum). The superior cerebellar peduncle is more superior. The mesencephalic nucleus of V is in the midbrain. Medial and inferior vestibular nuclei are in the upper medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Lower pons: middle cerebellar peduncle. Midbrain: superior cerebellar peduncle. Medulla: inferior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.text: About substantia nigra, all true except:
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra is present DORSAL to the cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri), not ventral. It consists of pars compacta (dopaminergic neurons) and pars reticularis. It is connected to the basal ganglia circuit. Its dopamine content gives it its dark color.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia nigra: dorsal to crus cerebri, contains dopamine, connected to basal ganglia.

questions.text: The tract in MLB responsible for head righting reflex is:
questions.explanation: The interstitiospinal tract (from interstitial nucleus of Cajal) is primarily responsible for the head righting reflex, which maintains head position in space. The tectospinal tract is for neck reflexes in response to visual stimuli. Vestibulospinal maintains posture. Reticulospinal for autonomic functions.
questions.keyConcept: Interstitiospinal tract: from interstitial nucleus of Cajal, head righting reflex, descends in MLF.

questions.text: Mention 3 external feature of the ventral surface of the pons.
questions.explanation: The ventral surface of the pons shows: the basilar groove (lodging the basilar artery), the middle cerebellar peduncle (lateral), and transverse grooves between bundles of transverse pontine fibers. The pons has two parts: basilar (anterior) and tegmental (posterior).
questions.keyConcept: Ventral pons: basilar groove (basilar artery), MCP laterally, transverse pontine fiber bundles.
questions.modelAnswer: Middle cerebellar peduncle (on each side), basilar artery sulcus (central groove), and transverse grooves between bundles of transverse pontine fibers. These features reflect the pontine structure with its basilar and tegmental portions.

questions.text: What are the lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle are: superiorly = the superior cerebellar peduncle; inferiorly = the inferior cerebellar peduncle plus the gracile and cuneate tracts; laterally = the lateral recess (extending toward the cerebellum).
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle lateral boundaries: superior = SCP, inferior = ICP + gracile/cuneate tracts, lateral recess.
questions.modelAnswer: Superiorly: superior cerebellar peduncle. Inferiorly: inferior cerebellar peduncle and the gracile and cuneate tracts. The lateral boundary also includes the lateral recess, which extends toward the cerebellopontine angle.

questions.text: What does the medial medullary syndrome cause?
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (due to anterior spinal artery occlusion) causes: contralateral hemiplegia (corticospinal tract), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue paralysis (CN XII nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiplegia + proprioception loss, ipsilateral tongue paralysis.
questions.modelAnswer: Contralateral flaccid hemiplegia (corticospinal tract), contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral lower motor neuron paralysis of the tongue (hypoglossal nucleus damage).

questions.text: Concerning the fourth ventricle; choose the most correct answer:
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle roof is formed by the superior cerebellar peduncle (superior medullary velum) and inferior medullary velum, not the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof
options: Its floor is formed by the closed medulla and pons.
Its roof is formed by the superior and inferior medullary vela.
Its choroids plexus is present in the floor of the ventricle.
It has a communication with the lateral ventricle.

questions.text: A 25‑year‑old woman presents with proximal, jerky, non‑purposeful movements of the limbs accompanied by hypotonia. Degeneration of which central nervous system structure is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Chorea (jerky, non-purposeful movements) with hypotonia results from caudate nucleus degeneration in Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant condition.
questions.keyConcept: Chorea pathophysiology
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord

questions.text: Which receptors are most likely responsible for the sudden muscle relaxation when a weight‑lifter releases a heavy load after a sustained hold?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs (type Ib) detect muscle tension and trigger inverse stretch reflex causing sudden muscle relaxation when tension becomes dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon reflex

questions.text: 3 external features of ventral pons:
questions.explanation: The ventral pons displays three characteristic features: the middle cerebellar peduncle laterally, the basilar artery groove centrally, and transverse grooves indicating underlying fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral pons features: middle cerebellar peduncle, basilar groove, transverse fibers.
questions.modelAnswer: MCP, Basilar artery sulcus, transverse grooves.

questions.text: Which of the following thalamic nuclei has a motor function?
questions.explanation: The ventral lateral (VL) thalamic nucleus is the primary motor relay nucleus. It receives input from the cerebellum (via dentatothalamic tract) and basal ganglia (via medial globus pallidus internus) and projects to the motor cortex. It helps coordinate voluntary movement planning and execution.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral lateral (VL) nucleus is the motor relay nucleus of the thalamus; receives cerebellar and basal ganglia input.

questions.text: Which of the following thalamic nuclei relays motor impulses?
questions.explanation: The ventral anterior (VA) nucleus is a motor-related thalamic nucleus that receives input from the basal ganglia (via the medial globus pallidus internus) and projects to the premotor and motor cortices. It plays a role in motor planning and initiation. VA and VL together form the motor thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral anterior (VA) nucleus relays motor impulses from basal ganglia to motor cortex.

questions.text: Describe non-specific thalamic nuclei.
questions.explanation: Non-specific (intralaminar) thalamic nuclei include the centromedian, parafascicular, and intralaminar nuclei. They receive input from the reticular formation, cerebellum, and spinal cord, and project diffusely to the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia. They are involved in arousal, attention, and pain perception, maintaining wakefulness and regulating level of consciousness.
questions.keyConcept: Non-specific thalamic nuclei (intralaminar) project diffusely to cortex; regulate arousal, attention, and pain perception.
questions.modelAnswer: Non-specific (intralaminar) thalamic nuclei include the centromedian nucleus, parafascicular nucleus, and intralaminar nuclei. They lack specific cortical projections and instead send diffuse projections to association cortices. Input sources: reticular formation (brainstem), cerebellum, and spinal cord. Functions: (1) Regulation of arousal and alertness—part of the ascending reticular activating system. (2) Pain modulation—receive pain input and project to somatosensory cortex. (3) Cognition and attention—integrate brainstem and cerebellar signals with cortical activity. (4) Part of the circuits involved in autonomic control. They are distinct from specific relay nuclei which have precise topographic connections.

questions.text: Describe how unconscious proprioception is carried to cerebellum.
questions.explanation: Unconscious proprioception reaches the cerebellum via spinocerebellar tracts: From lower body: Muscle spindles/Golgi tendon organs → dorsal root ganglion (1st neuron) → Clarke's nucleus in posterior horn (2nd neuron) → posterior spinocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum. From upper body: Same pathway but accessory cuneate nucleus → cuneocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle. These tracts carry proprioceptive information for motor coordination without conscious awareness.
questions.keyConcept: Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum via spinocerebellar tracts through inferior cerebellar peduncle
questions.modelAnswer: Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum: (1) From lower body: Muscle spindles/Golgi tendon organs → dorsal root ganglion (1st) → Clarke's nucleus (2nd) → posterior spinocerebellar tract (or anterior) → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum. (2) From upper body: Same → accessory cuneate nucleus (2nd) → cuneocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum.

questions.text: Which of the following fibers carry proprioception from the upper limb to the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb to the cerebellum. It originates from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus) and enters through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries upper limb proprioception

questions.text: Afferent fibers in the superior cerebellar peduncle include:
questions.explanation: The anterior (ventral) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the lower body to the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle. It decussates twice (once at the level of entry and once before entering the cerebellum).
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinocerebellar enters via superior cerebellar peduncle

questions.text: The inferior cerebellar peduncle contains:
questions.explanation: The posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information from the lower body to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. It does not decussate.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinocerebellar tract via inferior cerebellar peduncle

questions.text: Superior cerebellar peduncle contains which of the following tracts?
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle contains the ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract which carries proprioceptive feedback from the lower limbs to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle contains ventral spinocerebellar

questions.text: The most lateral nucleus in the interior of the cerebellum is:
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus is the largest and most lateral cerebellar nucleus. It receives input from the cerebellar cortex (particularly the lateral parts) and projects via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the thalamus and red nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Dentate nucleus is most lateral, projects via SCP

questions.text: The nucleus that projects neocerebellar efferent is the:
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus is the main output nucleus of the neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres). It projects inhibitory fibers via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral thalamus (VPL/VPM) and red nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Dentate nucleus projects neocerebellar efferent

questions.text: Thalamic nucleus that relays cerebellar output:
questions.explanation: The ventral lateral thalamic nucleus receives input from the deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose nuclei) via the superior cerebellar peduncle and dentatothalamic tract. It then projects to the motor and premotor cortices, serving as the cerebellar relay to the cerebrum.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral lateral nucleus relays cerebellar output to the cerebral cortex.

questions.text: The thalamic nucleus that relays cerebellar fibers to the cerebral cortex is the:
questions.explanation: The ventral lateral (VL) nucleus is the principal relay nucleus for cerebellar output destined for the cerebral cortex. It receives input from the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle and dentatothalamic tract, and projects to the motor and premotor cortices, influencing voluntary movement.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral lateral nucleus relays cerebellar fibers from the dentate nucleus to the motor cortex.

questions.text: Thalamic nucleus that relays basal ganglia output:
questions.explanation: The ventral anterior (VA) nucleus is the thalamic relay for basal ganglia output. It receives input from the internal segment of the globus pallidus (medial GPi) and projects to the premotor and supplementary motor cortices. This pathway is important for motor planning and sequencing of movements.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral anterior nucleus relays basal ganglia output (from GPi) to premotor cortex.

questions.text: Which of the following cerebellar parts has mainly spinal connections:
questions.explanation: The spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate zones) has mainly spinal connections - receives proprioceptive input from spine, controls axial and limb movement.选项B正确. The answer is B. Vestibulocerebellum has vestibular connections; cerebrocerebellum has cerebral connections.
questions.keyConcept: Spinocerebellum (vermis) has spinal connections - receives proprioceptive input, controls axial muscle tone.

questions.text: What are the parts of neostriatum?
questions.explanation: The neostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen. Together with the globus pallidus, these form the corpus striatum. The caudate and putamen are separated by the internal capsule but are functionally connected.
questions.keyConcept: Neostriatum: caudate nucleus + putamen. Striatum = neostriatum + paleostriatum (globus pallidus).
questions.modelAnswer: Caudate nucleus and putamen. These are the input nuclei of the basal ganglia, receiving cortical input. They are separated by the internal capsule but functionally linked as the striatum.

questions.text: What are the parts of paleostriatum?
questions.explanation: The paleostriatum (globus pallidus) consists of two parts: the internal (medial) segment (GPi) and external (lateral) segment (GPe). GPi is the main output nucleus; GPe is part of the indirect pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Paleostriatum: globus pallidus internal (GPi) + external (GPe). GPi = output; GPe = indirect pathway.
questions.modelAnswer: Globus pallidus external (GPe) and globus pallidus internal (GPi). The external segment is part of the indirect pathway; the internal segment is the main output of the basal ganglia.

questions.text: What is the blood supply of basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus) are supplied by central branches of the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery. The lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) are the primary supply.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia: supplied by lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) and anterior cerebral artery branches.
questions.modelAnswer: Central branches of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, particularly the lenticulostriate arteries which penetrate the basal ganglia through the anterior perforated substance.

questions.text: What is the venous drainage of basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia drain into veins that empty into the thalamostriate vein (also called terminal vein), which then drains into the internal cerebral veins and ultimately the great cerebral vein (Galen) into the straight sinus.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia venous drainage: thalamostriate vein → internal cerebral veins → great cerebral vein → straight sinus.
questions.modelAnswer: Veins that drain into the thalamostriate vein, which courses through the basal ganglia region and empties into the internal cerebral veins, then to the great cerebral vein of Galen.

questions.text: What are the 3 lobes of the cerebellum (Functional classification)?
questions.explanation: The three functional lobes of the cerebellum are: archicerebellum (vestibulocerebellum - flocculonodular lobe), paleocerebellum (spinocerebellum - vermis and paravermis), and neocerebellum (cerebrocerebellum - lateral hemispheres).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar functional lobes: archi (vestibular), paleo (spinal), neo (cerebral).
questions.modelAnswer: Archicerebellum (flocculonodular lobe - vestibular connections), paleocerebellum (vermis and paravermis - spinal connections), and neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres - cerebral cortex connections).

questions.text: What is the archicerebellum formed of?
questions.explanation: The archicerebellum consists of the flocculus (paired lateral structures) and nodule (median part of inferior vermis). It is the oldest part of the cerebellum (phylogenetically) and is connected to the vestibular system.
questions.keyConcept: Archicerebellum: flocculus + nodule. Oldest part, vestibular connections, maintains balance.
questions.modelAnswer: The flocculus (paired lateral structures) and nodule (median part of the inferior vermis). These structures form the flocculonodular lobe, which receives primary vestibular input.

questions.text: What is the paleocerebellum formed of?
questions.explanation: The paleocerebellum consists of the vermis (median zone) and paravermal (intermediate) zones of both cerebellar hemispheres. It receives proprioceptive input from the spinal cord and controls axial and proximal limb movements.
questions.keyConcept: Paleocerebellum: vermis + paravermis. Receives spinal input, controls axial/proximal movement.
questions.modelAnswer: The vermal part and the two paravermal parts of the cerebellar hemisphere. The vermis controls axial muscles; paravermis controls proximal limb muscles. Both receive proprioceptive input from the spinal cord.

questions.text: Mention the 4 cerebellar nuclei.
questions.explanation: The four deep cerebellar nuclei (medial to lateral) are: fastigial nucleus (most medial), globose nucleus, emboliform nucleus, and dentate nucleus (most lateral, largest). The dentate nucleus is the main output nucleus, projecting via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar nuclei (medial to lateral): fastigial, globose, emboliform, dentate. Dentate = main output.
questions.modelAnswer: Dentate nucleus (largest, most lateral), emboliform nucleus, globose nucleus, and fastigial nucleus (most medial). The dentate nucleus is the main output, while the fastigial nucleus influences vestibular and eye movements.

questions.text: Which tract passes through the superior cerebellar peduncle?
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle contains primarily efferent fibers from the dentate nucleus to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus (dentatorubrothalamic pathway), carrying cerebellar output.
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle is the major output pathway from cerebellum to forebrain.

questions.text: Which fibers enter the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle?
questions.explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries afferent fibers including the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's column), cuneocerebellar fibers, and vestibulocerebellar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior cerebellar peduncle is primarily afferent, carrying proprioceptive and vestibular information to cerebellum.

questions.text: Which fibers are afferent to cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle?
questions.explanation: Afferents through the inferior cerebellar peduncle include: dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's column), cuneocerebellar fibers from accessory cuneate nucleus, and vestibulocerebellar fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior cerebellar peduncle carries proprioceptive and vestibular afferents to cerebellum.

questions.text: Which structure of the basal ganglia is classified as the paleostriatum?
questions.explanation: The globus pallidus internus (GPi) and externus (GPe) together form the paleostriatum (old striatum), while the putamen and caudate nucleus form the neostriatum (new striatum).
questions.keyConcept: Paleostriatum refers to the globus pallidus, distinguished from the neostriatum (caudate-putamen).

questions.text: Which structure is part of the neostriatum?
questions.explanation: The neostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen (also called the striatum). It receives cortical input and dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra pars compacta.
questions.keyConcept: Neostriatum comprises caudate and putamen, the major input structures of the basal ganglia.

questions.text: Purkinje cells are stimulated by the following except:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are excited by climbing fibers, mossy fibers (indirectly via granule cells), and parallel fibers; basket and Golgi cells provide inhibitory input.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cell inputs

questions.text: Regarding the cerebellum, choose one correct answer:
questions.explanation: The spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate hemisphere) regulates muscle tone and coordination; the neocerebellum plans movement and the paleocerebellum controls equilibrium.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar functional divisions
options: Middle cerebellar peduncle connects it to medulla oblongata.
Paleocerebellum is concerned with planning and programming movement.

questions.text: Parts of neostriatum:
questions.explanation: The neostriatum (striatum proper) consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen, separated by the internal capsule but functionally interconnected as part of the basal ganglia motor loop.
questions.keyConcept: Neostriatum = caudate nucleus + putamen.
questions.modelAnswer: The neostriatum (striatum) consists of the putamen and caudate nucleus, separated by the internal capsule. It is the major input structure of the basal ganglia, receiving cortical, dopaminergic (from substantia nigra pars compacta), and thalamic inputs. It projects GABAergic neurons to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra.

questions.text: Parts of paleostriatum:
questions.explanation: The paleostriatum refers to the globus pallidus, which is divided into internal (GPi) and external (GPe) segments that serve as the main output nuclei of the basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Paleostriatum = globus pallidus internus and externus.
questions.modelAnswer: Globus pallidus internal and external.

questions.text: Blood supply of basal ganglia:
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia receive blood supply from central branches of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, which penetrate the brain substance to supply the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia supplied by branches of anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
questions.modelAnswer: Central branches of anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

questions.text: Venous drainage of basal ganglia:
questions.explanation: The thalamostriate vein drains the basal ganglia and thalamus, carrying blood to the internal cerebral vein and ultimately the vein of Galen.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamostriate vein provides venous drainage for basal ganglia.
questions.modelAnswer: The venous drainage of the basal ganglia is via the striate veins (thalamostriate veins), which drain into the internal cerebral veins and then the great cerebral vein (of Galen). These veins ultimately drain into the straight sinus. The basal ganglia also drain via the basal vein to the great cerebral vein.

questions.text: Archicerebellum formed of:
questions.explanation: The archicerebellum, the oldest functional region, is formed by the flocculi and nodule, which together constitute the vestibular cerebellum controlling balance and eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: Archicerebellum = flocculus and nodule of inferior vermis.
questions.modelAnswer: 2 flocculi and nodule (part of inferior vermis).

questions.text: Paleocerebellum formed of:
questions.explanation: The paleocerebellum, controlling posture and gait, is formed by the vermal portion and paravermal zones of the cerebellar hemispheres, receiving proprioceptive input from the body.
questions.keyConcept: Paleocerebellum = vermis and paravermal zones for postural control.
questions.modelAnswer: Vermal part and 2 paravermal parts of cerebellar hemisphere.

questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia modulate movement through indirect and direct pathways that influence thalamic output to the motor cortex, without directly executing voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia: modulate movement and motor learning, not direct execution.
options: Modulation of movement and motor learning

questions.text: Primary integrative neuron of cerebral Cortex:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are the primary integrative neurons of the cerebellar cortex, receiving input from climbing and parallel fibers and outputting via their axons to deep nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje cell function

questions.text: As regards the pyramidal tract, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The corticospinal fibers descend as scattered bundles in the basis pontis because they are interrupted by transverse pontine fibers. This is a normal anatomical feature of the pontine base.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal scattered in pons by pontine fibers
options: It arises from motor area 4 only.
It passes through anterior limb of internal capsule.
It descends within the medial 3/5 of basis pedunculi.
It descends as scattered bundles in basis pontis.
Its crossed fibers in medulla form anterior corticospinal tract.

questions.text: Upper motor neuron lesion is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Positive Babinski sign (dorsiflexion of big toe with fanning) is a hallmark of upper motor neuron lesion, indicating corticospinal tract damage and release of primitive reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Positive Babinski indicates UMN lesion
options: Paralysis of muscle & all types of movement.

questions.text: Lower motor neuron lesion is characterized by:
questions.explanation: LMN lesion causes lost/absent tendon jerks due to direct muscle denervation, muscle atrophy, and loss of all muscle tone and reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: LMN lesion causes lost tendon jerks

questions.text: Describe termination of pyramidal tract.
questions.explanation: The pyramidal tract terminates on anterior horn cells: The lateral corticospinal tract terminates on alpha motor neurons (final common pathway) and gamma motor neurons in the anterior horn of all spinal segments. The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed, small) terminates similarly but only in upper cervical segments. Corticobulbar fibers terminate on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal tract terminates on anterior horn motor neurons; corticobulbar terminates on brainstem motor nuclei
questions.modelAnswer: Termination of pyramidal tract: The lateral corticospinal tract terminates on alpha motor neurons (final common pathway) and gamma motor neurons in the anterior horn of all spinal segments. The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed) terminates similarly but only in upper segments. Corticobulbar fibers terminate on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem.

questions.text: Give an account on differences between upper & lower motor neuron lesions.
questions.explanation: UMN vs LMN lesion differences: UMN lesions cause spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Babinski sign, and no muscle atrophy (or minimal). LMN lesions cause flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, hyporeflexia/areflexia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and no Babinski sign. UMN affects descending corticospinal pathways; LMN affects the peripheral motor neurons or their cell bodies.
questions.keyConcept: UMN: spastic, hyperreflexia, Babinski positive, no atrophy. LMN: flaccid, areflexia, atrophy, fasciculations
questions.modelAnswer: UMN vs LMN lesion differences: (UMN) Spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Babinski, no muscle atrophy (or minimal); (LMN) Flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, hyporeflexia/areflexia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, no Babinski. UMN lesion affects descending corticospinal pathways; LMN affects peripheral motor neurons or their cell bodies.

questions.text: The anterolateral boundary of interpeduncular fossa is formed by:
questions.explanation: The crus cerebri (basis pedunculi) forms the anterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. It contains the corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Crus cerebri forms anterolateral boundary of interpeduncular fossa

questions.text: Acute-stage upper motor neuron lesions result in:
questions.explanation: In the ACUTE stage of upper motor neuron lesion, there is FLACCID paralysis (not spastic) due to spinal shock—loss of all reflexes and tone below the lesion. This phase lasts days to weeks. Later, as spinal shock resolves, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and Babinski sign develop. The answer choice D (flaccid paralysis) describes the acute UMN lesion phase.
questions.keyConcept: Acute UMN lesion = FLACCID paralysis (spinal shock); chronic UMN lesion = spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign.

questions.text: Mention 2 extrapyramidal tracts.
questions.explanation: The two major extrapyramidal tracts (motor pathways outside the corticospinal tract) are the tectospinal tract (from superior colliculus, controls neck muscles) and the rubrospinal tract (from red nucleus, controls limb flexor muscles).
questions.keyConcept: Extrapyramidal tracts: tectospinal (neck control), rubrospinal (flexor muscles). Both modulate movement.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Tectospinal tract - originates from superior colliculus, crosses in dorsal tegmental decussation, descends to cervical spinal cord to control neck and upper trunk muscles in response to visual stimuli. 2) Rubrospinal tract - originates from red nucleus, crosses in ventral tegmental decussation, descends to control flexor muscles of the upper limb.

questions.text: What is the lamination of pyramidal tract in the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: In the internal capsule, the pyramidal tract fibers are organized with fibers for facial muscles in the genu (knee), upper limb fibers most anterior in the posterior limb, and lower limb fibers most posterior in the posterior limb.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule pyramidal tract: genu = face, anterior posterior limb = upper limb, posterior posterior limb = lower limb.
questions.modelAnswer: Fibers for face muscles are in the genu; upper limb area lies most anterior and lower limb area lies most posterior in the posterior limb of internal capsule. This anterior-to-posterior arrangement in the posterior limb represents head-to-toe body map.

questions.text: Upper motor neuron lesion is characterized by
questions.explanation: UMN lesion is characterized by spasticity (hypertonia), hyperreflexia, Babinski sign (plantar extension), and retained muscle bulk initially; option E (plantar flexion) describes normal reflex.
questions.keyConcept: UMN lesion characteristics
options: Plantar flexion of big toe on scratching skin of sole

questions.text: Lower motor neuron lesion is characterized by
questions.explanation: LMN lesion is characterized by flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, muscle wasting, fasciculations, decreased/absent reflexes, and no Babinski sign (plantar reflex absent or normal flexion).
questions.keyConcept: LMN lesion characteristics

questions.text: Which extrapyramidal tract helps adjust the head and neck in response to visual and cutaneous stimuli?
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract originates from the superior colliculus and carries reflexes related to head and neck movement in response to visual stimuli, decussating at the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract mediates reflex head movements toward visual stimuli, crossing at midbrain level.

questions.text: Which descending motor pathway serves as an alternate route to the corticospinal tract?
questions.explanation: The rubrospinal tract originates from the red nucleus, decussates immediately, and descends in the lateral funiculus. It serves as an accessory pathway for corticospinal function, particularly for flexor muscle control.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract is a crossed extrapyramidal pathway for motor control of distal limbs.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an extrapyramidal tract?
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract is the main pyramidal tract for voluntary movement. The reticulospinal, rubrospinal, and vestibulospinal tracts are extrapyramidal. The tectospinal tract is also extrapyramidal.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal tracts are the only major pyramidal motor pathways; all others are extrapyramidal.

questions.text: Dorsal spinocerebellar enters cerebellum through ............. while ventral spinocerebellar through.............
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle while the ventral spinocerebellar tract enters via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar peduncle entries
options: Superior cerebellar peduncle, inferior cerebellar peduncle
inferior cerebellar peduncle, superior cerebellar peduncle

questions.text: 2 extrapyramidal tracts:
questions.explanation: The two main extrapyramidal tracts are the reticulospinal tract (medial and lateral) and the vestibulospinal tract (lateral and medial).
questions.keyConcept: Extrapyramidal tracts
questions.modelAnswer: Rubro-spinal tract and vestibulo-spinal tract.

questions.text: Lamination of pyramidal tract in internal capsule:
questions.explanation: In the internal capsule, the pyramidal tract is arranged: anterior limb (frontal connections), genu (face), posterior limb (arm, leg) from front to back.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal internal capsule
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior limb: frontal; Genu: face; Posterior limb: arm above, leg below.

questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the extrapyramidal tracts?
questions.explanation: Extrapyramidal tracts (rubrospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, tectospinal) influence muscle tone, posture, and automatic movements rather than fine skilled movements controlled by the pyramidal system.
questions.keyConcept: Extrapyramidal tracts: regulate posture and muscle tone.
options: They originate exclusively from the motor cortex.
They are concerned with fine skilled movements.
They influence posture and muscle tone.
They decussate only in the medulla.

questions.text: Which tract is the main alternative (indirect) pathway to the corticospinal tract for motor control?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus/rubrospinal tract is the principal alternative motor pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract: main indirect pathway from cerebellum via red nucleus to spinal cord.

questions.text: Describe roof of 4th ventricle.
questions.explanation: The roof of the fourth ventricle has two layers: (1) SUPERIOR MEDULLARY VELUM - connects the superior cerebellar peduncles, contains lingula and central lobule of cerebellum; (2) INFERIOR MEDULLARY VELUM - stretches between the two inferior cerebellar peduncles; (3) The fastigium marks the apex of the roof. The roof is completed by the cerebellar vermis and its white matter. Choroid plexus protrudes through the lateral apertures.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof: superior and inferior medullary vela, fastigium (apex), cerebellar vermis
questions.modelAnswer: STRUCTURES IN TEGMENTUM PONTIS: (1) CRANIAL NERVE NUCLEI: Abducent, facial, vestibulocochlear; (2) TRACT: Medial longitudinal fasciculus; (3) LEMNISCI: Medial lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus; (4) NUCLEI: Superior olivary, cochlear, vestibular, nuclei of reticular formation; (5) PYRAMID does NOT continue here (interrupted by transverse fibers).

questions.text: Describe lateral boundaries of 4th ventricle.
questions.explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle: (1) SUPERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - forms the upper lateral boundary; (2) MIDDLE CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - forms the lateral boundary at mid-pontine level; (3) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - forms the lower lateral boundary; (4) FLOOR of lateral recess. The lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) are located at the lateral extremities. The peduncles connect the cerebellum to the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle lateral boundaries: superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles at different levels
questions.modelAnswer: CRUS CEREBRI CONTENTS: (MEDIAL 1/5) Frontopontine fibers; (MIDDLE 3/5) Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers; (LATERAL 1/5) Parietopontine and temporopontine fibers. The corticospinal fibers are somatotopically organized with arm fibers anterior to leg fibers.

questions.text: A 32‑year‑old woman has difficulty writing, right arm weakness, and reduced light touch on the left leg. CSF shows elevated IgG, mononuclear cells, and oligoclonal bands. Which pathologic finding is most likely?
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis shows perivascular lymphocytic cuffing with demyelinated axons in white matter and oligoclonal IgG bands in CSF.
questions.keyConcept: Multiple sclerosis pathology
options: Perivascular lymphocytes with demyelinated axons in white matter
Multinucleated cells in grey and white matter

questions.text: A 32‑year‑old woman has right arm weakness and reduced light touch on the left leg. CSF shows oligoclonal bands. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis presents with oligoclonal bands in CSF, periventricular white matter lesions, and relapsing-remitting neurological deficits.
questions.keyConcept: Multiple sclerosis diagnosis

questions.text: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by the union of which veins?
questions.explanation: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins, which drain the deep brain structures including the basal ganglia and thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Vein of Galen forms from union of internal cerebral veins draining deep brain structures.
options: Right and left internal cerebral veins

questions.text: Anterior spinal artery occlusion:
questions.explanation: Anterior spinal artery occlusion produces bilateral upper motor neuron signs below the lesion and bilateral loss of pain/temperature with preserved proprioception due to intact posterior columns.
questions.keyConcept: ASA occlusion: bilateral motor loss, pain loss, preserved proprioception.
questions.modelAnswer: Bilateral UMNL below lesion, bilateral loss of pain and temperature, preservation of proprioception and touch.

questions.text: The Charcot's artery is the largest branch of ……… set of central branches of circle of Willis.
questions.explanation: Charcot's artery (also called the artery of cerebral hemorrhage) is the largest anterolateral central branch of the circle of Willis, supplying the internal capsule and basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Charcot's artery: largest anterolateral central branch of circle of Willis.

questions.text: A 42-year-old right-handed male arrives to the emergency department and is intoxicated. At the time of presentation, he is unable to move his hands and arms. The following day, once he is sober, a more thorough neurological examination reveals a complete flaccid paralysis of the upper limbs and severely diminished-to-absent reflex activity. What is the most likely area of spinal damage?
questions.explanation: This question appears to reference a spinal cord cross-section image showing different horn regions. Area C corresponds to the anterior horn where lower motor neurons reside. Damage to anterior horn cells at C8 level (or nearby) causes flaccid paralysis of the upper limbs with areflexia due to LMN destruction. This is consistent with anterior cord syndrome from watershed infarction, commonly seen after cardiac arrest or severe hypotension. The flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes indicate LMN, not UMN lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn cell damage causes flaccid paralysis with areflexia due to destruction of lower motor neurons.

questions.text: Pontine hemorrhage causes:
questions.explanation: Pontine hemorrhage typically damages bilateral corticospinal and autonomic pathways, causing pinpoint pupils (loss of pupillary light reflex), hyperpyrexia (autonomic dysregulation), and quadriplegia.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine hemorrhage: pinpoint pupils, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia.
questions.modelAnswer: Pinpoint pupil, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia.

questions.text:
Receptor/s for proprioception is/are:
I. Pacinian corpuscle.
II. Meissner’s corpuscle.
III. Ruffini’ corpuscle.
questions.explanation: Ruffini's corpuscles (type II slowly adapting mechanoreceptors) are proprioceptors in joints and skin. Pacinian corpuscles are vibration/pressure receptors, not proprioceptors.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioceptors: muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, Ruffini's (joints). Vibration: Pacinian. Light touch: Meissner's.

questions.text: All about muscle spindle true except:
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles contain intrafusal muscle fibers (not collagen fibers primarily). The capsule encloses the spindle but the internal structure is muscle fiber-based. They are in parallel with extrafusal fibers, have gamma efferents, and are encapsulated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: parallel with extrafusal fibers, contains intrafusal muscle fibers, encapsulated, gamma innervation.
options: Present in parallel with sk. Muscle fibers.

questions.text: Which of the following is a character of muscle spindle:
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles are innervated by both afferent (Ia, II) and efferent (gamma) nerve fibers. They contain intrafusal muscle fibers (not collagen), are in parallel with extrafusal fibers, respond to stretch, and are encapsulated.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle: parallel arrangement, intrafusal fibers, afferent + efferent innervation, stretch receptor.
options: Present In series with muscle fibers.
Innervated by afferent & efferent nerve fiber.

questions.text: One of the following is a character of lumbar level of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The lumbar spinal cord has the smallest white matter/grey matter ratio because it contains a large amount of grey matter (lower motor neurons for legs) relative to white matter (mostly descending tracts passing through). It has lateral horns for sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar cord: large grey matter (LMN for lower limb), small white/grey ratio, lateral horns present.

questions.text:
Which of the following is/are true for central nervous system?
I. It is rich in connective tissue cells.
II. It is soft jelly like.
III. It has grey matter and white matter.
questions.explanation: CNS is NOT rich in connective tissue - it is poor in CT, derived mainly from neuroectoderm. It IS soft and jelly-like (due to high water content), and has grey and white matter.
questions.keyConcept: CNS: poor in CT, soft/jelly-like (high water), has grey (neurons) and white (myelinated) matter.

questions.text: The processes of protoplasmic astrocytes characterized by:
questions.explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (in grey matter) have numerous short branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (in white matter) have few long unbranched processes. Both types express GFAP and have foot processes on blood vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: grey matter, numerous short processes. Fibrous astrocytes: white matter, few long processes.

questions.text: Cells of Cajal are present in
questions.explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the MOLECULAR layer of the CEREBRAL cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface. In cerebellum, this layer contains Purkinje cells, not Cajal cells.
questions.keyConcept: Cajal cells: horizontal cells in molecular layer of cerebral cortex; horizontal axon orientation.

questions.text: Climbing fibers:
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers are the axons of contralateral inferior olivary nucleus neurons. They ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle and climb on Purkinje cell dendrites. They carry error signals for motor learning. Mossy fibers (not climbing) end in granular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fibers: olivocerebellar (contralateral ION), climb on Purkinje dendrites, carry error signals.

questions.text: Accessory cuneate nucleus give rise to:
questions.explanation: The accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus gives rise to UNCROSSED fibers that ascend through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to reach the cerebellum (cuneocerebellar tract). These carry proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus: uncrossed fibers → cerebellum via ICP; proprioception from upper limb.

questions.text: Inferior olivary nucleus:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus receives input from the red nucleus (rubro-olivary fibers). It is located in the OPEN medulla, not ventral aspect. Its efferent fibers decussate and reach the CONTRALATERAL cerebellar cortex through the INFERIOR cerebellar peduncle as climbing fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary: receives rubral input, in open medulla, projects via ICP to contralateral cerebellum as climbing fibers.
options: Present in the ventral aspect of closed medulla.
Its efferent fibers reach the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
Its efferent fibers are the mousy fibers reaching the cerebellar cortex.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the grey matter?
questions.explanation: Grey matter in the spinal cord is located centrally (not outside white matter), composed mainly of nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers. It is surrounded by white matter and contains neuroglia.
questions.keyConcept: Grey matter is centrally located, formed mainly of nerve cells (not outside white matter)
