questions.text: One of the following drugs could be used sublingually in treatment of migraine attacks:
questions.explanation: Ergotamine is available as sublingual tablets for acute migraine treatment. Triptans (like sumatriptan) are available as nasal spray, subcutaneous injection, and oral tablets, but not typically sublingual. Topiramate (C) is a prophylactic, not acute treatment. Acetaminophen (D) is oral, not sublingual. The answer is A - ergotamine sublingual tablets are a recognized formulation for migraine treatment. questions.text: The following antipsychotic drug is preferred in children suffering from autism:
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole is an atypical antipsychotic with a favorable side effect profile, making it suitable for children with autism spectrum disorders. It has lower EPS risk and less sedation than older antipsychotics. Olanzapine (A) causes significant weight gain/metabolic syndrome. Quetiapine (C) has significant sedation. Thioridazine (D) has cardiac toxicity. Aripiprazole is FDA-approved for irritability in autism in children. Its partial agonist activity at D2 and 5-HT1A receptors provides efficacy with tolerability. The answer is B - aripiprazole is preferred for autism-related irritability.
questions.keyConcept: Aripiprazole is FDA-approved for autism irritability in children due to its favorable efficacy and side effect profile.

questions.text: Which drugs are classified as opioid antitussives?
questions.explanation: Opioid antitussives include: codeine and dextromethorphan. These act on the cough center in the medulla. Codeine is a weak opioid agonist used for cough and pain. Dextromethorphan is a non-opioid that acts on sigma receptors and NMDA receptors.选项C正确. The answer is C. These are central cough suppressants.
questions.keyConcept: Codeine and dextromethorphan are opioid antitussives acting on the medullary cough center.

questions.text: Which drugs are classified as opioid antidiarrheals?
questions.explanation: Opioid antidiarrheals include: loperamide (Imodium), diphenoxylate (with atropine as Lomotil), and opium tincture. These act on mu receptors in the myenteric plexus, decreasing motility and secretion.选项C正确. The answer is C. Loperamide does not cross BBB significantly, avoiding CNS effects.
questions.keyConcept: Loperamide and diphenoxylate are opioid antidiarrheals - mu receptor agonists in the gut decreasing motility.

questions.text: What is the cause of iatrogenic Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic Parkinson's disease is caused by drugs that block dopamine receptors: antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, risperidone), antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), and some calcium channel blockers.选项A正确. The answer is A. Drug-induced parkinsonism is reversible upon drug discontinuation but may take weeks to months.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) cause iatrogenic parkinsonism - reversible upon discontinuation.

questions.text: What is the aim of drug therapy in Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: The aim of drug therapy in Parkinson's disease is to restore dopamine deficiency and reduce excess cholinergic activity. This involves: dopamine replacement (L-dopa, dopamine agonists), COMT inhibitors (entacapone), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline), and anticholinergics for tremor.选项A正确. The answer is A. Treatment aims to improve motor symptoms and quality of life.
questions.keyConcept: PD drug therapy aims to restore dopaminergic activity and reduce cholinergic excess - improving motor function.
options: To restore balance between dopamine and acetylcholine activity in the basal ganglia
To increase dopamine activity in the basal ganglia
To decrease acetylcholine activity in the basal ganglia

questions.text: What are the first choice agents in early Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: First choice agents in early Parkinson's disease: levodopa/carbidopa combinations (most effective for motor symptoms) and dopamine agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole) as alternatives. MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline) may be used early.选项D正确. The answer is D. Treatment choice depends on age, symptom severity, and cognitive status.
questions.keyConcept: Levodopa/carbidopa and dopamine agonists are first-line for early PD - L-dopa is most effective, agonists delay motor complications.

questions.text: What are the classifications of local anesthetics?
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics classified by: 1) Chemical structure - esters (procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine) and amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine); 2) Duration of action - short, intermediate, long-acting.选项C正确. The answer is C. Esters are metabolized by plasma cholinesterase; amides are metabolized in liver.
questions.keyConcept: Local anesthetics are classified as esters vs amides (metabolism) and by duration of action (short/intermediate/long).

questions.text: Why are vasoconstrictors added to local anesthetics?
questions.explanation: Vasoconstrictors (epinephrine, norepinephrine, felypressin) are added to local anesthetics to: constrict blood vessels, reduce bleeding, decrease systemic absorption, prolong anesthetic duration, and reduce peak plasma levels.选项C正确. The answer is C. Contraindicated in patients with cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, and those on non-selective beta-blockers.
questions.keyConcept: Vasoconstrictors prolong local anesthetic duration and reduce toxicity by decreasing systemic absorption and bleeding.
options: To prolong the duration of action
To reduce systemic adverse effects and bleeding tendency

questions.text: How do general anesthetics inhibit neuronal activity?
questions.explanation: General anesthetics inhibit neuronal activity by enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission (GABA-A receptor activation - barbiturates, benzodiazepines, propofol, isoflurane) or inhibiting excitatory neurotransmission (NMDA receptor blockade - ketamine, nitrous oxide).选项C正确. The answer is C. Some agents do both. The net effect is decreased neuronal excitability and consciousness.
questions.keyConcept: General anesthetics enhance GABA (inhibitory) or block NMDA (excitatory) to inhibit neuronal activity.
options: They facilitate inhibitory effects of GABA at GABA receptors
Inhibit excitatory effects of glutamate at NMDA receptors

questions.text: What are the classic antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation: Classic antiepileptic drugs include: phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproic acid, ethosuximide, phenobarbital, and benzodiazepines. These are first-generation drugs with well-established efficacy.选项D正确. The answer is D. They have more drug interactions and side effects compared to newer agents.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, ethosuximide are classic antiepileptics - more side effects and interactions than newer drugs.

questions.text: What are the newer antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation: Newer antiepileptic drugs include: lamotrigine, levetiracetam, topiramate, gabapentin, pregabalin, vigabatrin, tiagabine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide, and zonimide. These have improved side effect profiles.选项D正确. The answer is D. They are often used as adjuncts or alternatives to classic drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Lamotrigine, levetiracetam, topiramate are newer antiepileptics - better tolerated with fewer drug interactions.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of antidepressants?
questions.explanation: Antidepressants work mainly by increasing synaptic monoamine levels (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine). SSRIs inhibit serotonin reuptake; SNRIs inhibit both; TCAs inhibit norepinephrine and serotonin; MAOIs inhibit monoamine oxidase.选项C正确. The answer is C. The monoamine hypothesis suggests depression involves decreased serotonin/norepinephrine.
questions.keyConcept: Antidepressants increase synaptic monoamines (serotonin, norepinephrine) via reuptake inhibition or enzyme blockade.
options: Increase brain biogenic amines (norepinephrine and serotonin)

questions.text: Which class of antidepressants is reserved for atypical depression associated with anxiety and phobia?
questions.explanation: MAO inhibitors (MAOIs) like phenelzine, tranylcypromine are reserved for atypical depression associated with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, and mood reactivity.选项A正确. The answer is A. They require dietary restrictions (tyramine avoidance) due to hypertensive crisis risk.
questions.keyConcept: MAOIs are reserved for atypical depression with hypersomnia and hyperphagia - require tyramine dietary restrictions.

questions.text: Which class of antidepressants is the first choice for initial therapy?
questions.explanation: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram) are first-choice for initial therapy due to: efficacy, once-daily dosing, safety in overdose, and favorable side effect profile.选项B正确. The answer is B. They are better tolerated than TCAs and MAOIs.
questions.keyConcept: SSRIs are first-line antidepressants - safe, effective, once-daily, and favorable side effect profile.

questions.text: Which class of antidepressants is reserved for resistant cases?
questions.explanation: MAOI antidepressants are reserved for resistant cases that fail other antidepressants. They require careful monitoring and dietary restrictions.选项C正确. The answer is C. They are used when SSRIs, SNRIs, and TCAs have failed due to their complexity and risk.
questions.keyConcept: MAOIs are reserved for treatment-resistant depression - require tyramine diet and careful monitoring.

questions.text: What is the aim of management for Alzheimer disease?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's management aims to: slow cognitive decline, manage behavioral symptoms, improve quality of life, and support caregivers. Options include cholinesterase inhibitors, memantine, and behavioral interventions.选项C正确. The answer is C. There is no cure - treatment is symptomatic.
questions.keyConcept: Alzheimer's treatment aims to slow progression and manage symptoms - cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are mainstays.
options: Increase cholinergic activity in the brain
Reduce excitotoxicity action of overstimulation of NMDA receptors

questions.text: What are the cholinesterase enzyme inhibitors used in the treatment of Alzheimer disease?
questions.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors for Alzheimer's: donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), galantamine (Razadyne). These increase acetylcholine in the brain.选项D正确. The answer is D. They provide modest symptomatic benefit.
questions.keyConcept: Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine are cholinesterase inhibitors - modestly effective in Alzheimer's.

questions.text: What are the first-line therapy drugs used in the treatment of MS?
questions.explanation: First-line MS disease-modifying drugs: interferon-beta preparations (Avonex, Betaseron, Rebif), glatiramer acetate (Copaxone). These reduce relapse rate by ~30%.选项A正确. The answer is A. They are injectables with modest efficacy.
questions.keyConcept: Interferon-beta and glatiramer are first-line MS disease-modifying therapies - reduce relapse rate ~30%.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of typical antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) work by blocking D2 dopamine receptors, reducing dopaminergic transmission in mesolimbic pathway (treats positive symptoms).选项A正确. The answer is A. Also blocks D2 in nigrostriatal pathway (causes EPS) and tuberoinfundibular pathway (hyperprolactinemia).
questions.keyConcept: Typical antipsychotics block D2 receptors - therapeutic for psychosis but cause EPS and hyperprolactinemia.
options: Blocking D2 receptors in the mesolimbic system improves positive symptoms

questions.text: What receptors do atypical antipsychotics block in addition to D2 receptors?
questions.explanation: Atypical antipsychotics (clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone) block D2 plus serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. This 5-HT2A blockade allows more dopamine in nigrostriatal pathway, reducing EPS.选项A正确. The answer is A. This dual blockade gives atypicals their improved side effect profile.
questions.keyConcept: Atypical antipsychotics block both D2 and 5-HT2A receptors - greater dopamine in motor pathways reduces EPS.

questions.text: What are the typical antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Typical antipsychotics include: haloperidol, chlorpromazine, thioridazine, fluphenazine, perphenazine, and flupentixol.选项D正确. The answer is D. They have high D2 affinity and significant EPS risk.
questions.keyConcept: Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, thioridazine are typical antipsychotics - high EPS risk from D2 blockade.

questions.text: What are the atypical antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Atypical antipsychotics include: clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, ziprasidone, aripiprazole, paliperidone.选项D正确. The answer is D. They have lower EPS risk but metabolic side effects.
questions.keyConcept: Clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone are atypicals - lower EPS but weight gain, metabolic syndrome risk.

questions.text: What are the risks of chronic abuse of opioids?
questions.explanation: Chronic opioid abuse risks: respiratory depression, dependence/addiction, constipation, hormonal dysfunction (hypogonadism), hyperalgesia, and infections (HIV, hepatitis from IV use).选项D正确. The answer is D. Opioid tolerance develops, requiring higher doses.
questions.keyConcept: Chronic opioid abuse causes respiratory depression, dependence, constipation, hormonal dysfunction, and infection risk.

questions.text: How is opioid abuse managed?
questions.explanation: Opioid abuse management: detoxification (methadone, buprenorphine maintenance), behavioral therapy, naltrexone (opioid antagonist) to prevent relapse, and support groups.选项D正确. The answer is D. Methadone maintenance is gold standard for opioid dependence.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid dependence: methadone/buprenorphine maintenance, naltrexone, behavioral therapy - comprehensive approach.

questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning anesthetics is correct ?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that blocks NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) glutamate receptors, producing anesthesia with catatonia and analgesia. Thiopental is short-acting due to redistribution, not metabolism; propofol lacks analgesic effect; halothane increases ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine as NMDA receptor antagonist producing dissociative anesthesia
options: Thiopental is ultra short acting due to rapid metabolism.
Propofol possesses a strong analgesic effect.
Halothane is the least likely inhalation agent to increase intracranial tension.
Dissociative anesthesia is induced by midazolam.

questions.text: The following concerning antiparkinsonian drugs is/are CORRECT?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is given subcutaneously in Parkinson's disease emergencies (e.g., akinetic crisis), and amantadine can cause insomnia. Carbidopa does not reduce L-dopa-induced dyskinesia (dopamine agonists do). Benztropine is an anticholinergic for tremor, not fluctuations. Answer E (A and D) is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine SC in emergency; amantadine-induced insomnia in Parkinson's treatment
options: Apomorphine is given subcutaneously in emergency.
L-dopa- induced dyskinesia is reduced by carbidopa.
Benztropine reduces fluctuations in response to L-dopa.

questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding NSAIDs is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Aspirin is contraindicated in children with viral infections due to Reye's syndrome risk; paracetamol or ibuprofen are preferred. All other statements about NSAIDs (nephrotoxicity, no respiratory depression, no dependence, GI irritation) are true.
questions.keyConcept: Aspirin contraindication in children (Reye's syndrome risk) making the statement FALSE
options: Nephrotoxicity may occur on chronic use of high doses
Respiratory depression seen with opioid analgesics does not occur with therapeutic doses of NSAIDs
Their use does not result in drug dependence seen with opioid analgesics
Aspirin is a good choice for use as analgesic antipyretic for children
They may cause-gastric mucosal irritation and bleeding

questions.text: Which of the following analgesic agents poses a risk in a 60-year-old patient with a history of transient ischemic attacks
questions.explanation: Celecoxib (a COX-2 inhibitor) increases cardiovascular risk (thrombotic events, stroke) in patients with prior TIA or stroke history. Paracetamol and aspirin are safer options in such patients, with aspirin having protective antiplatelet effects.
questions.keyConcept: COX-2 inhibitors contraindicated in patients with prior TIA/stroke history

questions.text: Which of the following is FALSE concerning selective COX 2 inhibitors ? :
questions.explanation: COX-2 inhibitors were withdrawn (rofecoxib) or carry warnings due to increased cardiovascular risk (heart attack, stroke). They do have low GI ulceration risk and nephrotoxicity concerns. Celecoxib is contraindicated in sulfonamide allergy.
questions.keyConcept: COX-2 inhibitors carry significant cardiovascular risk (heart attack, stroke) - FALSE statement
options: Are associated with low risk of gastric ulceration
Have a low risk of cardiotoxicity and stroke
Nephrotoxicity is a serious adverse effect
Celecoxib should not be given to patients with sulfonamide allergy

questions.text: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is not an enzyme inducer?
questions.explanation: Valproate is not a CYP enzyme inducer; it actually inhibits some cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are all enzyme inducers that increase metabolism of other drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate is NOT an enzyme inducer (unlike phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital)

questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement regarding antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation: Pregnant women with epilepsy should NOT discontinue antiepileptic drugs abruptly - the risk of seizures may outweigh the risks of the medication. Treatment should be continued with the lowest effective dose of the safest drug.
questions.keyConcept: Pregnant women should NOT discontinue AEDs abruptly (risky to mother and fetus) - FALSE
options: Females who get pregnant should discontinue the antiepileptic drug
They are contraindicated in neuropathic pain
Carbamazepine antagonizes the action of antidiuretic hormone

questions.text: Which of the following anesthetic agents is not acting through increase GABA activity?
questions.explanation: Ketamine acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, not through GABA enhancement. Halothane, propofol, and isoflurane all enhance GABA-A receptor activity (inhibitory neurotransmitter).
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine acts on NMDA receptors, not through GABA enhancement

questions.text: The following antiepileptic drug is not an enzyme inducer:
questions.explanation: Valproate is not a CYP enzyme inducer; it actually inhibits some cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are all potent enzyme inducers.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate NOT an enzyme inducer (inhibits CYP enzymes)

questions.text: Which opioid is a long‑acting, pure agonist associated with milder withdrawal symptoms?
questions.explanation: Methadone is a long-acting pure mu-opioid agonist used in opioid maintenance therapy, producing milder withdrawal due to its slow dissociation from receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Methadone pharmacology

questions.text: Which opioid acts as a partial agonist at the μ receptor and is used in opioid dependence management?
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist and kappa antagonist, producing ceiling effects on respiratory depression and milder withdrawal.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine mechanism

questions.text: An alcoholic patient shows dependence related to activation of opioid receptors. Which drug is used for treatment?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid antagonist used to prevent relapse in alcohol dependence by blocking opioid receptors involved in reward pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Naltrexone for alcoholism

questions.text: Which anti‑Parkinsonian drug commonly produces atropine‑like adverse effects (dry mouth, blurred vision)?
questions.explanation: Benztropine is an anticholinergic anti-Parkinsonian drug that produces peripheral atropine-like side effects including dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention.
questions.keyConcept: Anticholinergic Parkinson drugs

questions.text: Which drug is used as a rescue therapy to manage sudden episodes of motor deterioration in Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is a rapid-acting dopamine agonist used subcutaneously as rescue therapy for sudden off episodes (akinesia) in advanced Parkinson's disease.
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine rescue therapy

questions.text: Which drug is used for tremors (in Parkinson’s)?
questions.explanation: Benztropine (anticholinergic) is particularly effective for tremor in Parkinson's disease, acting by blocking excessive cholinergic activity in the striatum.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonian tremor treatment

questions.text: What happens when there are elevated levels of excitatory amino acids?
questions.explanation: Elevated excitatory amino acids (especially glutamate) cause excitotoxicity via excessive calcium influx, activating destructive enzymes, generating free radicals, and leading to neuronal death; implicated in stroke and neurodegenerative diseases.
questions.keyConcept: Excitotoxicity mechanism
questions.modelAnswer: Neurotoxicity resulting in neuronal death or injury

questions.text: What are neurodegenerative diseases?
questions.explanation: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons that are typically related by FUNCTION, not necessarily physical location. Example: Parkinson's affects dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra that form a functional circuit. Option A correctly states 'related by function, rather than physical location' - this is the definition. Option B says 'physical location' only - not accurate. Option C says 'function and physical location' - not precise. Option D says 'all neurons' - incorrect (neurodegenerative diseases are selective). The answer is A. Examples: Alzheimer's (cholinergic neurons), Parkinson's (dopaminergic neurons), Huntington's (GABAergic neurons) - all functionally related.
questions.keyConcept: Neurodegenerative diseases selectively destroy neurons that share functional characteristics, not necessarily physical proximity.
options: Disorders characterized by the cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons that are typically related by function, rather than physical location in the brain.
Disorders characterized by the cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons that are typically related by physical location in the brain.
Disorders characterized by the cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons that are typically related by function and physical location in the brain.
Disorders characterized by the cellular degeneration of all neurons.

questions.text: How are neurodegenerative diseases classified?
questions.explanation: Neurodegenerative diseases are classified by multiple methods including clinical presentation, protein type, pathological processes, and genetic abnormalities. Option E (likely meaning all of the above or a combination) is probably correct. A) Clinical presentation - yes (motor, cognitive, psychiatric); B) Type of protein - yes (alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's, tau in Alzheimer's, huntingtin in Huntington's); C) Pathological processes - yes (protein misfolding, aggregation); D) Genetic abnormalities - yes (APP, presenilin mutations in familial AD; LRRK2 in PD). The answer is E - all these classification schemes are used. Modern classification combines clinical, pathological, and genetic features.
questions.keyConcept: Neurodegenerative diseases are classified by clinical presentation, protein type (synuclein, tau, huntingtin), pathology, and genetics.

questions.text: What is the term for small infarcts in deep non-cortical white matter or the brainstem that result from the occlusion of penetrating branches of cerebral arteries?
questions.explanation: Lacunar infarcts are small deep infarcts in penetrating artery territories causing 'lacunes.' They result from lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries. These small vessel strokes affect basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, pons. Option A is CORRECT. They differ from cortical infarcts (B) which affect the cortex. The answer is A. Lacunar strokes are associated with hypertension and diabetes.
questions.keyConcept: Lacunar infarcts are small, deep infarcts from lipohyalinosis of penetrating arteries - associated with hypertension.

questions.text: A 58-year-old hypertensive patient presents with sudden onset of hemiplegia followed by symptoms of increased intracranial tension (headache & vomiting). A CT scan shows extensive intracerebral hemorrhage in the region of basal ganglia. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are small aneurysms that form on small penetrating arteries in hypertensive patients, most commonly affecting the basal ganglia (lenticulostriate arteries) and causing hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.
questions.keyConcept: Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in basal ganglia

questions.text: Pilocytic astrocytoma is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a WHO grade I tumor (benign) with good prognosis. Characteristic features: occurs in children (most common pediatric brain tumor), commonly arises in cerebellum (though can occur elsewhere), often cystic with a mural nodule. Option D states 'bad prognosis' which is INCORRECT - pilocytic astrocytoma has excellent prognosis with complete surgical resection (5-year survival >90%). This is the EXCEPT question, so D is the answer. In contrast, diffuse astrocytoma (grade II) and anaplastic astrocytoma (grade III) have progressively worse prognoses.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a benign childhood cerebellar tumor with excellent prognosis after complete resection.

questions.text: What imaging studies are mandatory for Multiple Sclerosis diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MRI of the brain is MANDATORY for MS diagnosis - it shows plaques as hyperintense lesions on T2/FLAIR images. CT scan (B) is not sensitive for MS. PET (C) and ultrasound (D) are not primary diagnostic tools. MRI demonstrates dissemination in space (multiple lesions) and time (gadolinium enhancement of active lesions). The answer is A. McDonald criteria require MRI evidence of CNS lesions.
questions.keyConcept: MRI brain is essential for MS diagnosis, demonstrating white matter lesions that fulfill dissemination in space and time.

questions.text: Muscle paralysis in case of poliomyelitis is due to:
questions.explanation: Poliovirus selectively destroys anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) in the spinal cord, causing flaccid paralysis. The muscle paralysis is NOT due to direct viral damage to muscle or toxin production.
questions.keyConcept: Polio paralysis from destruction of anterior horn motor neurons in spinal cord
options: Destruction of the muscle fibers by the toxins of the organisms.
Inflammation of the nerves supplying the affected muscles.
Degeneration of their anterior horn cells in the spinal cord.

questions.text: Poliomyelitis is usually an infection of:
questions.explanation: Poliovirus specifically infects and destroys anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) of the spinal cord, causing flaccid paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Polio pathogenesis
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
Posterior horn cells of the spinal cord

questions.text:
Diagnosis is of rabies in an infected animal can be done by 

A) Detection of specific antibodies in the serum 
B) Detection of Negri bodies in the brain tissue 
C) Both of them 
D) None of them
questions.explanation: Diagnosis of rabies in an infected animal is done by detecting Negri bodies in brain tissue. Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies found in neurons (especially in hippocampus and Purkinje cells of cerebellum) - they contain viral nucleoproteins. A) Detection of antibodies in serum - not reliable for animal diagnosis; B) Detection of Negri bodies - CORRECT; C) Both - incorrect because serum antibodies alone aren't diagnostic. The answer is B. In humans, PCR of saliva or nuchal biopsy is preferred. Animal diagnosis typically requires brain tissue examination.
questions.keyConcept: Negri bodies (eosinophilic inclusions in neurons) are pathognomonic for rabies in animal brain tissue.
options: Detection of specific antibodies in the serum
Detection of Negri bodies in the brain tissue
